title: Pediatric Nystagmus
subject: Paediatrics
summary: Nystagmus is an involuntary rhythmic eye movement that can signal vestibular, cerebellar or drug toxicity problems in children. In low‑resource settings, focus on bedside assessment and common tropical causes. Early recognition prevents visual loss and identifies life‑threatening central lesions.

sections.p: Nystagmus is a repetitive, involuntary eye movement that may be horizontal, vertical or torsional. Diagnosis is clinical: observe direction, amplitude, frequency, and whether it changes with gaze or position.
b: Horizontal: most common, often peripheral vestibular.
Vertical or direction‑changing gaze‑evoked: suggests central pathology.

sections.p: Severity is graded by impact on visual function and ability to maintain fixation. Use the Nystagmus Severity Scale (0‑4) where 0 = no functional impairment and 4 = severe oscillopsia with loss of fixation.
b: Stage 0: absent or subclinical.
Stage 1: mild, patient compensates.
Stage 2: moderate, reading difficulty.
Stage 3: severe, functional blindness.
Stage 4: disabling, requires surgical or optical intervention.

sections.p: In African paediatric practice, prioritize common infectious, metabolic and structural causes, then rarer genetic or drug‑induced etiologies.
b: Peripheral vestibular: otitis media, labyrinthitis, malaria‑related vestibulopathy.
Central cerebellar: cerebellar abscess, tuberculous meningitis, posterior fossa tumor.
Metabolic/toxic: antiepileptic drug excess, quinine toxicity, vitamin B12 deficiency.
Congenital: infantile nystagmus syndrome, albinism, cerebral palsy.
Systemic: HIV encephalopathy, sickle‑cell vaso‑occlusive cerebellar infarct.

sections.p: Parents notice a child’s eyes moving rhythmically, often with head thrusts to dampen motion. The child may have poor visual tracking, reading difficulty, or oscillopsia.
b: Horizontal jerk with fast phase away from fixation.
Vertical or torsional beats raise suspicion for central disease.
Accompanying signs: ataxia, dysmetria, vomiting, headache, fever.

sections.p: Use bedside tests first; order imaging only when central signs are present or the cause is unclear.

t.b: Is the nystagmus present in primary gaze only or does it appear on lateral gaze? → Peripheral if only primary, central if gaze‑evoked.
Abnormal (catch‑up saccade) suggests peripheral vestibular lesion.
Look for optic atrophy, papilledema, or retinal disease that may explain visual loss.
Detect posterior fossa tumor, cerebellar abscess, tuberculoma. If unavailable, refer to nearest centre.
Elevated levels confirm drug‑induced nystagmus; treat toxicity.

t.a: CBC, malaria rapid test, HIV rapid test
t.b: Identify infectious contributors common in low‑resource settings.

b: Acute onset with vomiting, headache, or altered consciousness.
Vertical or direction‑changing gaze‑evoked nystagmus.
Associated focal neurological deficits.
Rapid visual deterioration.

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first; then address the nystagmus itself with visual aids or therapy.
b: Infection: give appropriate antimalarial, antibiotics or anti‑TB therapy.
Drug toxicity: stop or reduce offending AED, monitor serum levels.
Cerebellar abscess: surgical drainage + broad‑spectrum antibiotics.
Congenital: refer to ophthalmology for prisms, low‑vision aids, and orthoptic therapy.
Supportive: educate caregivers on head‑turn strategies, use of tinted lenses to reduce oscillopsia.

sections.p: Regular review of visual function and neurological status; ensure vaccination and malaria prophylaxis to reduce preventable causes.
b: Re‑examine eye movements every 3‑6 months.
Monitor growth and development; intervene early with physiotherapy if ataxia persists.
Educate families on avoiding ototoxic drugs and ensuring adherence to antiretroviral therapy.

sections.p: Conditions that mimic nystagmus may lead to misdiagnosis.
b: Strabismus – misalignment without rhythmic movement.
Oscillopsia from vestibular loss – patient reports motion but eyes are not moving.
Seizure‑related eye flutter – brief, not rhythmic.

sections.p: Be aware of false‑negative or misleading findings.
b: Normal MRI does not exclude early cerebellar infection; repeat if symptoms evolve.
Serum drug levels may be normal in chronic toxicity; rely on clinical picture.

whenToSeekHelp: Acute vomiting, headache, or loss of consciousness with nystagmus
Rapid visual loss or new focal neurological signs

faq.q: Why is vertical nystagmus more concerning than horizontal?
faq.a: Vertical or direction‑changing beats usually arise from central brainstem or cerebellar lesions, which can be life‑threatening.
Yes, especially phenobarbital, phenytoin and carbamazepine at toxic levels; stopping or adjusting the drug often resolves it.
No, it can be transient when caused by infection or drug toxicity; congenital forms may persist but can be managed with visual aids.

exam: A 4‑year‑old with cerebral palsy presents with horizontal eye oscillations – what bedside tests differentiate peripheral from central causes? — Perform gaze‑evoked testing and HIT; central signs include vertical or direction‑changing beats.

A child from a malaria‑endemic area develops new nystagmus and ataxia – what is your next investigation and why? — Order malaria rapid test and consider MRI if neurological signs persist; malaria can cause vestibular dysfunction.
You suspect drug‑induced nystagmus in a child on phenobarbital – how do you confirm and manage? — Check serum phenobarbital level; if high, reduce dose or switch drug, monitor for improvement.
A patient has vertical gaze‑evoked nystagmus and headache – which red flag does this represent and what is the urgent step? — Central cause; arrange urgent neuro‑imaging and neurosurgical referral.

Explain why an ophthalmology referral is essential in congenital nystagmus – what interventions can improve visual function? — Ophthalmology provides prisms, low‑vision aids, and orthoptic therapy to reduce oscillopsia.

During a ward round you find a child with nystagmus and papilledema – what underlying condition should you consider and what test is priority? — Raised intracranial pressure, likely due to posterior fossa mass; obtain urgent MRI or CT if MRI unavailable.
How does the Head Impulse Test help in evaluating nystagmus? — A corrective saccade indicates peripheral vestibular loss; a normal HIT with nystagmus suggests central origin.

What preventive measures reduce the incidence of infectious causes of nystagmus in low‑resource settings? — Ensure malaria prophylaxis, complete immunisation, prompt treatment of otitis media, and HIV testing/treatment.
